nutshell: Standard ReID (and even domain-generalized ReID) assumes train and test data share one object category, requiring a separate model per category (person, vehicle, etc.). This paper introduces Object-Generalized Re-Identification (OG-ReID): learning one category-agnostic identity representation that generalizes across heterogeneous object types. Their MGOR framework treats meta-learning not as adaptation but as distributional regularization - episodes are built with perturbed category mixtures (EDPS), the model must stay discriminative on the perturbed split without adapting (MOIL), and a dual global/category-local supervision head (HSE) balances cross-category invariance against within-category discrimination.
contributions: A new task formulation, OG-ReID, that distinguishes 'category shifts' (fundamentally different identity-defining visual cues across object types - body parts vs. geometric contours vs. texture patterns) from the appearance-level 'domain shifts' that existing DG-ReID work targets.

Episodic Distribution Perturbation Sampling (EDPS): builds category-balanced mini-batches and splits them into meta-train/meta-test halves with deliberately perturbed category composition per episode, unlike standard P×K sampling which leaves category mixture unconstrained during training.

Meta-Object Invariance Learning (MOIL): reframes meta-learning as a stability test rather than MAML-style adaptation - a single θ must remain discriminative on the perturbed meta-test split with no adaptation step, plus a Conditional Pairwise Alignment loss (1D sliced Wasserstein distance between meta-train/meta-test positive/negative distance distributions) to keep local discriminative geometry stable across the perturbation.

Hierarchical Semantic Equilibrium (HSE): two ViT class tokens (global category-agnostic + category-local) trained jointly in meta-train but validated only via the global token in meta-test and at inference, reconciling within-category discrimination and cross-category invariance through label-space factorization rather than explicit/adversarial alignment.

Trained on 5 single-category datasets (person, vehicle, vessel, two animal species) and evaluated zero-shot (no target-domain adaptation) across 9 diverse datasets spanning 100+ unseen categories - including wildlife, pet faces, generic objects, and even a geo-localization task - beating both domain-specific and domain-generalizable baselines, and a recent category-generalization competitor (VICP) that requires target-domain adaptation samples while MGOR needs none.
deficiencies: On MSMT17 - the most standard, best-understood benchmark in the whole evaluation suite, and a seen category (person) - a plain domain-specific baseline (CLIP-ReID) outright beats MGOR (Rank-1 43.4 vs. 41.3, mAP 19.4 vs. 18.1). The paper concedes this in the text but frames it as an acceptable trade-off, which means the flagship generalization method isn't the best choice on the single benchmark most readers will already have priors about.

Table 3's ablation shows nearly all of the improvement over the TransReID baseline comes from the first addition alone (EDPS & MOIL: e.g. MSMT17 mAP 14.2→16.2, PetFace mAP 31.5→40.5), while HSE's further contribution is comparatively small on several datasets (e.g. Wildlife71 mAP 85.3→86.0, ELPephants R1 36.5→38.6) - the text describes HSE as yielding 'the most significant overall improvement,' which overstates its marginal contribution relative to EDPS+MOIL on multiple of the six ablation datasets.

All five training categories come from a single, fairly narrow benchmark dataset each (Market-1501, VeRi, VesselReID, iPanda-50, ATRW), and much of the unseen-category evaluation also leans on similarly curated settings (PetFace pet portraits, CUTE lab-controlled objects) - there's no evaluation on uncontrolled, cluttered real-world multi-category imagery, so how far the reported generalization extends beyond benchmark-style photography is untested.

Fig. 5's own parameter analysis shows that increasing EDPS's category-disjoint probability actively hurts the seen-category benchmark (MSMT17) while helping multi-category evaluation - a genuine single-category-vs-multi-category trade-off baked into the method's core sampling hyperparameter - but the main results report only one fixed operating point, without guidance for a deployment that doesn't know in advance whether its test distribution will be single- or multi-category.
notable: The closest prior 'Generalizable Object ReID' competitor, VICP, needs a batch of target-domain images for in-context prompt adaptation and performs reasonably on single-category and even some multi-category settings (e.g. CUTE mAP 30.1) - but its Wildlife71 mAP collapses to just 1.2 (vs. MGOR's 86.0), a far more dramatic failure than the paper's summary phrase ('a pronounced drop in mixed category settings') conveys on its own; worth knowing since it shows target-adaptation-based generalization methods can fail catastrophically rather than gracefully outside their comfort zone.
